title: Java 21 Modern Features: Quick Revision
summary: Fast revision of the Java 21 language features that change everyday code: var, records, sealed classes, pattern matching, switch expressions, text blocks and virtual threads. Covers the mental model, usage, comparisons and the mistakes that cost marks in interviews.

chapters.title: var and Text Blocks
points: var is local variable type inference: the compiler infers the static type from the initializer, so the variable is still strongly typed (not dynamic)
var works only for locals, for-loop variables and lambda parameters; it is not allowed for fields, method parameters, return types, or without an initializer (var x; and var x = null; fail)
var list = new ArrayList<String>() infers ArrayList<String>, not List<String>; declare the interface type when you want to program to the interface
Text block: triple-quote """ delimiters, opening line break required; incidental indentation is stripped based on the least-indented line or the closing delimiter position
Text block gotchas: a trailing backslash joins lines, \s keeps a trailing space, a literal """ must be escaped, and .formatted(args) fills %s placeholders

chapters.title: Records
points: record Point(int x, int y) {} declares an immutable data carrier; the compiler generates a private final field per component, a canonical constructor, accessors x() and y() (no get prefix), equals, hashCode and toString
Compact canonical constructor has no parameter list and is used for validation or normalisation: record Range(int lo, int hi) { Range { if (lo > hi) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }
Records are implicitly final, cannot extend a class, cannot declare instance fields beyond the components, but can implement interfaces and declare static members and extra methods
Record vs Lombok @Value vs plain class: records are shallowly immutable, so a List component can still be mutated unless you copy it with List.copyOf in the compact constructor
Common mistake: expecting setters or inheritance; records suit DTOs, map keys and pattern-matching data, not JPA entities that need mutability or a no-arg constructor

chapters.title: Sealed Classes and Interfaces
points: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {} restricts which types may implement or extend it, giving a closed set of subtypes the compiler knows
Every permitted subclass must declare exactly one modifier: final (no further extension), sealed (continues the restriction) or non-sealed (reopens the hierarchy)
permits may be omitted when the subclasses are in the same source file; otherwise they must be in the same package (or same module if named) as the sealed type
Sealed vs final vs open: final allows zero subclasses, sealed allows a known list, open allows anyone; records are a natural fit as final permitted subtypes

Mistake: forgetting the final/sealed/non-sealed modifier on a permitted subclass causes a compile error, and adding a new permitted type breaks every non-exhaustive switch (which is the intended safety net)

chapters.title: Switch Expressions and Pattern Matching
points: Switch expression returns a value and uses arrow labels: int n = switch (day) { case MON, TUE -> 1; default -> 0; }; there is no fall-through and no break needed
Use yield to return a value from a block inside a switch expression; a switch expression must be exhaustive (cover every case or include default)
Pattern matching for instanceof: if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3) binds s with no cast; the binding is in scope only where the match is definitely true

Pattern matching for switch: case Circle c -> ..., case Square s -> ..., plus case null -> ... for null (a pattern switch otherwise throws NullPointerException on null) and guards written case Circle c when c.r() > 10 -> ...

Record deconstruction patterns: case Point(int x, int y) -> x + y; over a sealed hierarchy with no default the compiler checks exhaustiveness, and the order of cases matters because a dominated pattern is a compile error

chapters.title: Virtual Threads
points: Virtual threads (final in Java 21) are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier platform threads; when one blocks on I/O it unmounts and the carrier runs another, so you can have millions
Create them with Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable), Thread.startVirtualThread(r) or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() inside try-with-resources; the executor's close() waits for all tasks
Platform vs virtual: platform threads are 1:1 with OS threads and costly (about 1 MB stack), virtual threads are cheap and one per task; they help blocking I/O workloads, not CPU-bound work
Never pool virtual threads; create one per task, and limit concurrency to a resource with a Semaphore, not a pool size
Pinning gotcha: blocking inside a synchronized block (or native call) pins the virtual thread to its carrier in Java 21, so prefer ReentrantLock; also avoid heavy ThreadLocal data and long CPU loops

chapters.title: Java 21 Cheat Sheet
points: var: locals only, inferred static type, needs an initializer, never fields or parameters
record R(int a) {}: immutable, accessors a(), compact constructor for validation, final, can implement interfaces
sealed X permits A, B; subclasses must be final, sealed or non-sealed; enables exhaustive switch with no default
switch: arrows with no fall-through, yield in blocks, case null, guards with when, record patterns case P(int x, int y)
Text block """ ... """ strips incidental indent; virtual threads: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), one per task, never pooled, avoid synchronized around blocking calls
